questions.stem: One who speaks many languages is a:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'poly' = many + 'glotta' = tongue. Bilingual = two only; linguist is one who studies language (not necessarily speaks many).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: One who hates mankind is a:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'misos' = hate + 'anthropos' = human. Antonym = philanthropist (lover of mankind). Misogynist = hater of women specifically.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: A person who collects stamps is a:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'philos' (love) + 'ateleia' (exempt from tax — stamps were originally proof of paid postage). Numismatist collects coins; bibliophile loves books.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: A person who walks in sleep is a:
questions.explanation: L. 'somnus' = sleep + 'ambulare' = to walk. Soliloquist talks to oneself; insomniac cannot sleep; hypnotist induces trance.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: One who abstains totally from alcohol is a:
questions.explanation: From the 19th-century temperance movement — the 'T' was added to 'total' for emphasis ('T-total'). Distractor epicure is a lover of refined pleasure (esp. food).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: One who destroys cherished beliefs or institutions is an:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'eikon' (image) + 'klastes' (breaker) — literally an image-breaker (originally religious). Atheist denies God; agnostic says it's unknowable; anarchist opposes government.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: An expert judge of art, food, wine, or other matters of taste is a:
questions.explanation: Fr. 'connaître' = to know. A connoisseur has refined, authoritative taste. Gourmet also applies to food specifically; gourmand means a greedy eater, slight pejorative.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: One who copies another's work and claims it as their own is a:
questions.explanation: L. 'plagiarius' = kidnapper. A plagiarist steals intellectual content. Impostor pretends to be someone else; forger fakes documents.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: A person who lives in solitude away from society is a:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'eremos' = desert, deserted. Recluse is a close synonym. Nomad is a wanderer; aborigine is an original inhabitant; stoic endures without complaint.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: An absolute ruler with unchecked power is an:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'autos' = self + 'kratos' = rule. An autocrat rules alone with no accountability. Oligarch is one of a small ruling group; aristocrat is noble-born; plutocrat rules by wealth.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: A person who has an intense dislike or fear of people from other countries is called a:

options.option_text: Xenophobe — one who fears or dislikes foreigners intensely
Misogynist — one who harbours deep prejudice against women
Hypochondriac — one who imagines suffering from serious illness
Philanthropist — one who devotes personal resources to helping others

questions.explanation: 'Xenophobe' derives from Greek 'xenos' (stranger) + 'phobos' (fear), denoting extreme dislike or fear of foreigners. 'Misogynist' is a common wrong pick but refers specifically to hatred of women, not of foreign nationals.

questions.stem: A person with refined, sophisticated knowledge of fine food and the art of cuisine is called a:

options.option_text: Glutton — one who consumes food and drink to excess greedily
Epicure — one who dedicates themselves to refined sensory pleasure
Gourmet — one with cultivated and discerning taste in fine food
Ascetic — one who practises strict self-denial of all pleasures

questions.explanation: A 'gourmet' has expert, cultivated knowledge of food and cuisine — think food critic. 'Epicure' is the most tempting distractor but refers broadly to enjoyment of sensory pleasures beyond food; 'glutton' implies mindless excess without any refinement or knowledge.

questions.stem: A person whose chief aim in life is the active pursuit of pleasure and self-gratification is called a:

options.option_text: Stoic — one who endures pain or hardship without showing any emotion
Hedonist — one who believes pleasure is the highest good in life
Altruist — one who unselfishly dedicates efforts to the welfare of others
Nihilist — one who rejects all established religious and moral principles

questions.explanation: 'Hedonist' comes from Greek 'hedone' (pleasure); the philosophical position holds that pleasure is life's ultimate good. 'Nihilist' is a frequent wrong choice because it also sounds philosophical, but nihilism is about rejecting meaning/morality — not pursuing pleasure.

questions.stem: A person who deliberately pretends to be sick or injured in order to avoid duty or work is called a:

options.option_text: Misanthrope — one who distrusts and holds dislike for all of humanity
Recluse — one who chooses to withdraw and live in complete isolation
Malingerer — one who fakes illness deliberately to escape responsibilities
Dilettante — one who casually dabbles in the arts without real commitment

questions.explanation: 'Malingerer' precisely describes someone feigning illness to avoid duty — common in military and workplace contexts. The critical distinction from 'hypochondriac' (not listed here but frequently confused): a hypochondriac genuinely believes they are ill; a malingerer consciously deceives.

questions.stem: A person who travels regularly between different locations as part of their occupation, having no permanent base, is called an:

options.option_text: Nomad — one who moves seasonally following livestock or food resources
Vagabond — one who wanders aimlessly with no home or steady livelihood
Pilgrim — one who undertakes a long journey to a distant sacred place
Itinerant — one who travels between locations as an integral part of work

questions.explanation: 'Itinerant' (Latin 'itinerari', to travel) refers to a professional who moves between locations — itinerant judges, preachers, or tradespeople. 'Vagabond' implies aimless wandering without employment, while 'nomad' describes whole communities following traditional seasonal migration routes.

questions.stem: A person who has acquired deep, expert-level knowledge across a wide range of entirely different disciplines is called a:

options.option_text: Dilettante — one who maintains only a superficial interest in many subjects
Polymath — one with profound learning spread across many diverse disciplines
Virtuoso — one with outstanding technical mastery concentrated in a single art
Pedant — one who is excessively preoccupied with minor rules and details

questions.explanation: 'Polymath' (Greek: 'polys' = many + 'manthanein' = to learn) denotes a person of genuinely deep knowledge in multiple fields — Leonardo da Vinci is the textbook example. The most tempting distractor is 'dilettante', but a dilettante has only breadth without depth — the exact opposite of a polymath.

questions.stem: A person who makes a loudly aggressive display of patriotism and strongly advocates military confrontation with foreign nations is called a:

options.option_text: Nationalist — one who actively promotes the sovereign interests of their nation
Chauvinist — one who holds extreme and belligerent pride in their own country
Jingoist — one who loudly advocates an aggressive and belligerent foreign policy
Patriot — one who devotedly loves and willingly defends their home country

questions.explanation: 'Jingoist' derives from 'By Jingo!', a rallying cry from 19th-century British war-mongering debates; it specifically means someone who combines loud patriotism with demands for aggressive foreign military action. 'Chauvinist' is the strongest distractor but covers only extreme national pride — it need not involve advocating foreign confrontation.
